newsitem.title: GERMANY: Eastern German activists join Kohl's party.
newsitem.headline: Eastern German activists join Kohl's party.

text.p: Six eastern German civil rights activists joined Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservatives on Tuesday in a surprise move that highlighted the lingering problem German parties are having in dealing with communists in the east.

Vera Lengsfeld, a member of parliament for the Greens party, led six other eastern civil rights leaders into Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), saying the CDU was the only bulwark against communism.
Lengsfeld, the only member of parliament in the group, and the other six are little known outside political circles in Germany.
But the shift in party affiliation caused a sensation because of its implications for the next general election due in 1998.

In addition to the favourable media attention Lengsfeld's defection brings to the CDU, especially in the east where its support is weak, the shift increased the centre-right coalition's majority in parliament to 12 seats from 10.

"We entered politics in 1989 with the goal of getting the SED and its successor out of power," Lengsfeld said at a news conference in Berlin. "The ominous rapproachement with the PDS is something that we cannot accept."

Kohl's CDU has stood alone in its unwavering condemnation of the reform communist Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to Erich Honecker's iron-fisted SED party that nearly vanished in 1990 but has since rebounded to become the third strongest force in the east.
The SPD and Greens have ruled out entering an alliance on the federal level with the PDS, which won only 4.4 percent nationwide but picked up nearly 20 percent in the east.

But the two leftist parties have been cooperating with the PDS at the state and local level for years, raising fears among ardent anti-communists that the PDS could be part of a leftwing coalition after the next elections due in 1998.
"The step by Vera Lengsfeld and other prominent civil rights leaders marks a triumph for the CDU," said CDU general secretary Peter Hintze at a news conference in Bonn.
"These leaders of the peaceful revolution against the SED regime are saying that the CDU is the party that best represents the ideals of freedom."

Aside from Langsfeld, the new CDU members included Angelika Barbe, a co-founder of the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in East Germany, Guenther Nooke, former leader of the Brandenburg state Alliance fraction, Ehrhart and Hildigund Neubert, Wolfgang Kupke, and Markus Derling.
The Greens rejected Lengsfeld's charges and called on her to give up her seat in parliament. They also criticised her for strenghtening Kohl's fragile majority.
"I call on Vera Lengsfeld to return her Bundestag mandate," said the Greens leader Gunda Roestel. "It is a matter of political honesty and credibility."

Lengsfeld herself was a famous victim of the communist security apparatus under her married name Wollenberger. She found out in 1992 that her own husband Knud had for years spied on her for the ministry of state security. She divorced him and took back her maiden name.
